Uniform Approach at Kraft Heinz 

The Kraft Heinz PSM approach starts with identifying and understanding the process hazards associated with the technology of the process. From this, the design, operation, and maintenance of process equipment are structured to ensure its integrity. Policies, programs, procedures, and standard practices, are established to: 

 

Prevent and control accidental releases of hazardous materials or energy. 

Minimize the consequences of hazardous events which could result in human injury or illness, damage to property, or harm to the environment. 

 

All employees at the affected facilities need to understand their roles and responsibilities under the PSM program. It is especially important for managers and supervisors to not only understand and carry out their responsibilities under the PSM program, but also to continually educate the individuals in their areas in the relevant PSM Program elements. The affected employees are then trained in the potential hazards and procedures that will minimize the chance of process-related incidents and injuries. This interaction between people and technology is supported by programs and management oversight designed to ensure that aspects of the program remain effective and current. 

PSM Model 

ActiveX controlTo help understand the PSM concept and to provide a framework for the PSM program, it is useful to develop a general PSM model, as illustrated below in Figure 1. This figure illustrates the importance of integrating process technology knowledge, safety management, and the people involved with them to achieve effective process safety management. 

Figure 1. PSM Model 

 

More specifically: 

Process Technology includes equipment, chemistry, and materials associated with the Ammonia refrigeration process. 

Safety Management includes the procedures and safe work practices that ensure PSM goals are met. It also includes the policies and programs that ensure the people and processes work safely

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1.	Accidental Release Prevention and Emergency Response Policies
Kraft Heinz takes many precautions to prevent or minimize accidental releases of ammonia from the refrigeration system.  These precautions include safety controls (detection systems, alarms and automatic shutdown devices) which are designed to identify and prevent potentially unsafe conditions like pressure increases that could cause a system failure.  We also have a preventive maintenance program designed to maintain the on-going integrity of the systems and a training program designed to ensure that the systems are operated by qualified personnel.  All employees are informed of hazards in the workplace.  Employees who work with potentially hazardous substances receive proper training in the handling of those substances.  This facility has procedures in place to safely remove employees from areas in the unlikely event that a hazardous substance release were to occur, and to put in place emergency notification and response procedures.
2.	Facility and Regulated Substances
The Kraft Heinz facility located in Mason City, IA, is a production facility processing various food products. The regulated substance at this facility, anhydrous ammonia, is used in a closed-loop refrigeration system for product cooling and preservation in production and storage areas. In order to protect its employees, the public and the environment, an integrated safety management program has been established to prevent ammonia releases and mitigate the consequences of a release, should one occur.
3.	Worst Case and Alternative Case Release Scenarios
Off Site Consequence (OCA) data is available for review onsite at the Kraft Heinz facility.
4.	General Accidental Release Prevention Program and Ammonia Specific Prevention
The Kraft Heinz facility has an accidental release prevention program that complies with OSHAs Process Safety Management Standard and EPAs Risk Management Program Rule. The prevention program consi

sts of the following elements:
- Employee Participation Program
- Process Safety Information
- Process Hazard Analysis
- Operating Procedures
- Training Program
- Contractor Safety Program
- Pre-Startup Safety Review Procedures
- Mechanical Integrity Program
- Hot Work Permit Procedures
- Management of Change Procedures
- Incident Investigation Procedures
- Emergency Planning and Response
- Compliance Audit Procedures
The Kraft Heinz facility in Mason City, IA has an emergency action plan that addresses the response necessary for a release of ammonia from the refrigeration system. Because of the pungent odor of ammonia, any leak is easily detected.  The compressor room is provided with ammonia detectors that activate if ammonia is detected.  The refrigeration system is designed so that major components can be isolated by closing selected valves.  Further, refrigeration system operators have been trained and are knowledgeable in the safe operation of the refrigeration system.  In case of a release that could travel off the plant property, calls would be made to the Mason City, IA North Central Regional Emergency Response Commission Team and the Cerro Gordo County Emergency Management Agency (LEPC) to assist in the response.  Other state and federal notifications would be made as required.
5.	Five Year Accident History
There have been no reportable releases of ammonia in the past five years.
6.	Emergency Response Program
This Kraft Heinz facility has procedures in place to respond to the release of a hazardous substance.  Employees are trained to evacuate their respective areas in accordance with OSHA 1910.38(a). Kraft Heinz has also trained personnel in the Hazardous Waste Operation and Emergency Response Program, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120 HAZWAOPER. The trained personnel have been trained to the Technician Level Responder and also Incident Command training.  The trained personnel will assess each release situation and determine by the risk assessment the appropriate emer

gency response to initiate.  Coordination with the local fire department and outside emergency responders is initiated during an emergency situation.
7.	Planned Changes to Improve Safety
Kraft Heinz expects to improve safety performance by emphasizing all elements of its PSM/RMP program.  All recommendations during the Process Hazard Analysis were designed to improve the safety performance of the ammonia refrigeration process.  Kraft Heinz expects to evaluate each PHA and compliance audit recommendation in a timely manner and implement, as soon as possible, those recommendations that will reduce the possibility of a release and/or mitigate the consequences of an unintentional release.  A GAP Analysis is performed every five years to analyze current safety practices to current code to ensure the facility meets current code.

Kraft Heinz - Mason City Plant PSM Standard

Purpose 

This document provides an overview of the Kraft Heinz Standard for managing the operation and maintenance of the ammonia refrigeration systems in Kraft Heinz facilities across North America through the PSM system. Effective implementation of this standardized approach will: 



OSHA Standard 

Ensure the Kraft Heinz facility is meeting or exceeding the OSHA standard 29?CFR OSHA 1910.119. 

 

Safety and Performance 

Institutionalize an effective ammonia process management approach throughout Kraft Heinz that maximizes safety while optimizing program performance. 

Adherence to this Standard is essential. The safety of the public and Kraft Heinz employees is at stake, regulatory requirements must be complied with (and are subject to audit), our systems and processes will run more efficiently by using these standardized best practices, and our employees will be much better informed and trained. 

 

Audits, Reviews and Certification 

The facility PSM Coordinator will ensure the 3-Year PSM Compliance Audit at each facility are completed on time and all follow-up recommendations are implemented

in a timely manner. 

The facility PSM Coordinator will review and complete this Executive Summary with any new Facility Manager and/or Environmental Health and Safety Manager (EHS) within 60 days of the placement of the person in the position. After the initial review has been conducted, the PSM Coordinator will then be required to review and sign this Executive Summary with the Facility Manager and EHS Manager annually. The previous three years of signed Executive Summary documentation must be retained on file for future reference.  

 

Background 

Anhydrous ammonia is used as a refrigerant in a large number of industrial facilities. Ammonia is a toxic gas under ambient conditions and ammonia releases therefore have the potential for harmful effects on workers and the public. Many parts of these systems contain ammonia under pressure, which increases the risk since large quantities can be rapidly released. 

 

OSHA and EPA regulate facilities with large quantities of hazardous chemicals such as ammonia that meet a threshold quantity (TQ) (10,000lbs for ammonia). The Clean Air Act (CAA), as amended in 1990, requires the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to address concerns that chemical accidents could pose a risk to employees, the public, and the environment. The objective of these regulations is to prevent accidental chemical releases and minimize their impact if they do occur. 

 

The ammonia refrigeration process requires the transfer, use, and storage of ammonia and therefore involves a certain degree of risk, which must be minimized.  Process Safety Management (PSM), as described in 29 CFR OSHA 1910.119, involves the identification, understanding, and control of process hazards. The overall goal of the Kraft Heinz PSM program is to prevent process-related incidents and injuries associated with the accidental release of highly hazardous chemicals in the workplace or into the environment.

together. 

Personnel are those who operate, maintain, design, and otherwise support the Ammonia processes. 

Program Elements 

ActiveX controlThis program has been designed to comply with OSHA regulations and standards. The PSM model illustrated previously can now be expanded to address all of the elements of PSM identified in the regulations, as shown below in Figure 2. 

Figure 2. Regulatory 14 Elements of PSM Embedded in the Kraft Heinz PSM Model 

 

This model serves as a reminder that the 14 PSM elements that make up the PSM regulatory requirements work together in an integrated fashion. Kraft Heinz has structured a uniform, standardized approach for all of our ammonia refrigeration systems to meet or exceed the regulatory requirements and achieve maximum performance. 

 

The following are organized around the 14 PSM elements, addressed in the same order as they are presented in the regulatory requirements. 

Element 1-Employee Participation 

PSM must involve employees in all parts of the process. Participation by employees can make significant contributions toward a safer workplace. 

The Kraft Heinz standard approach includes roles and responsibility matrices to clearly define expectations for all employees (including management).  All employees will, at a minimum, receive training in awareness and the PSM elements. 

Specific procedures that are followed to define employee participation at the Kraft Heinz facility are contained in Element 1, Employee Participation. 

 

Element 2- 
Process Safety Information (PSI) 

 

The purpose of compiling written process safety information is to provide a resource for the process hazard analysis team and other employees involved with process safety by providing data concerning the potential hazards posed by the process. Process Safety Information includes the following information:  

Hazards of the chemicals used in the process. 

Process technology information (e.g., simplified process flow diagram, process chem

istry, max. intended ammonia inventory, safe upper/lower operating limits, evaluation of the consequences of deviation). 

Process equipment information (e.g., P&IDs, classifications, materials, safety relief design and design basis, ventilation system design, safety systems/devices, codes & standards). 

The process safety information must be updated whenever changes are made, and current information made available to employees. 

 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain Kraft Heinzs process safety information are contained in Element 2, Process Safety Information. 

 

Element 3- 
Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) 

A Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) is the heart of PSM. The PHA is a thorough, orderly, systematic approach for identifying, evaluating, and controlling potential hazards within a process involving hazardous chemicals such as ammonia. 

The Kraft Heinz PHA program includes: 

 

Addressing process hazards, previous incidents and near misses with catastrophic potential. 

All changes (MOCs, incident investigation, PHA, compliance audit changes) were made to the system since the last PHA was performed. 

Any incidents since the last PHA. 

Any recommendations from the last PHA. 

Element 3- 
Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) (continued) 

System to promptly address findings and recommendations, assure recommendations are resolved and documented, document action taken, develop a written schedule for completing actions, and communicate actions to operating, maintenance and other employees who work in the process or might be affected by actions 

Updating and revalidating PHAs at least every 5?years 

Retaining PHA records and updates for the life of the process 

 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain the Kraft Heinz PHA program are contained in Element 3, Process Hazard Analysis. 

 

Element 4 -Operating Procedures  

OSHA requires the development, implementation, and maintenance of clearly written, detailed proced

ures, and practices for the safe operation of the ammonia refrigeration process during all operating phases. The operating procedures provide employees involved in the operation of the ammonia refrigeration process with the written information and precautions necessary to safely perform their tasks in a consistent manner. 

Written procedures are required for start-up, normal operation, temporary operations, emergency shutdown, emergency operations, normal shutdown, and start-up following a turnaround or emergency shutdown. The operating procedures are required to address operating limits, including the consequences of deviations, steps to correct and/or avoid deviations, and safety systems and their functions.  

Operating procedures also address safety and health considerations regarding the process, including the properties and hazards of the chemicals used, the precautions necessary to prevent exposure, control measures to be taken if contact or exposure to the chemical occurs, and any special or unique hazards (such as high noise levels).  

Element 4 -Operating Procedures (continued) 

Safe work practices must be in place to provide for the control of hazards during operations including, but not limited to confined space entry, lockout/tagout, opening process equipment or piping, and control over entrance into facility by contractors, maintenance, laboratory, or other support personnel. 

Updates to the Operating Procedures are managed through the Management of Change (MOC) process, which requires that affected employees are involved in writing, reviewing, and educating one another on any change in procedures. Operating procedures must be certified annually that they are current and accurate.  

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain written operating procedures are contained in Element 4, Operating Procedures. 

 

Element 5 - Personnel Training and Performance  

All employees and contractors who operate an ammonia refrigeration system

must understand the safety and health hazards of ammonia and the refrigeration system. Employees and contractors who actually operate the system must understand how to do so. The training guideline describes the process by which personnel should operate and supervise the ammonia refrigeration system may be trained and qualified. 

The Kraft Heinz standard for training includes: 

 

Initial Training. 

Refresher Training. 

Classroom Training. 

On-the-Job Training (OJT). 

Training for Primary Operator. 

Training for Support Operator. 

Training for Production Ammonia Authorized. 

Training for Maintenance Ammonia Authorized. 

Training for Engineers, Supervisors, and Managers.  

Documentation and record keeping requirements. 

 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain required training programs at Kraft Heinz facilities are contained in Element 5, Training. 

 

Element 6 - Contractor Training and Performance 

The safety program for all contract employers must be evaluated by Kraft Heinz. The intent of the contractor safety element is to require employers who use contractors to perform work in and around processes that involve highly hazardous chemicals to establish a screening process so that they hire and use contractors who accomplish the desired job tasks without compromising the safety and health of employees at a facility. The contractor must assure that contract employees are trained on performing the job safely, the hazards related to the job, and applicable provisions of the emergency action plan. 

 

Kraft Heinz management must ensure that all contractor employees working at Kraft Heinz facilities are informed of certain hazards and the applicable portions of the emergency action plan, log contract employee injuries occurring during work involved in the covered process, evaluate the contractors safety performance while working onsite, and control contract employee access to the process. Contract employers must provide employe

e training and information concerning hazards, ensure that employees follow the employers safety rules, and alert the employer to hazards discovered during work or presented by the work the contract employees are performing. 

 

The contractor safety program applies to all contractors performing maintenance, repair, shutdown, major renovation, or specialty work on or adjacent to the ammonia process. 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain the Kraft Heinz contractor safety program are contained in Element 6, Contractors. 

 

Element 7 - PreStartup Safety Review (PSSR) 

The purpose for the prestartup safety review is to help ensure that safety, design, operation, maintenance and training have been addressed before ammonia is introduced into the system.  

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain the Kraft Heinz prestartup safety review program are contained in Element 7, PreStartup Safety Review. 

 

Element 8 -Mechanical Integrity 

To prevent or minimize the consequences of catastrophic releases of ammonia, it is important to ensure that ammonia refrigeration equipment is properly inspected, tested, and maintained. The purpose of the Kraft Heinz Mechanical Integrity (MI) program is to maintain ammonia refrigeration equipment so that a catastrophic release of ammonia is avoided, and, if necessary, properly contained. The emphasis should be on preventive maintenance rather than breakdown maintenance. 

Element 8 -Mechanical Integrity (continued) 

The MI program covers the specific pieces of equipment and system components that are to be maintained, the planned maintenance and quality assurance activities to be performed, inspection and testing procedures, training procedures, and documentation instructions. The equipment and system components covered by the MI program are those that contain ammonia, plus those key support or utility systems and equipment, which are considered critical to the safety and reliability o

f the ammonia system. 

 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain Kraft Heinzs Mechanical Integrity program are contained in Element 8, Mechanical Integrity. 

 

Element 9 - Hot Work Permit 

The purpose of the hot work permit procedure is to ensure that employees, contractors and company property are properly protected against fire, explosion, and other dangers resulting from hot work (cutting and welding and any other spark producing operation such as brazing, grinding, burning, and exposure of energized electrical conductors) in or near a process. 

 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain the KraftHeinz hot work permit guidelines are contained in Element 9, Hot Work Permit. 

 

Element 10 -Management of Change (MOC) 

Any facility or process is continually undergoing change. Changes may be made to improve the efficiency of the operation, improve the operability, and improve safety or to replace mechanical equipment.  Changes to process chemistry, technology, equipment, procedures, or facilities must be analyzed to ensure that existing safeguards against catastrophic releases are not compromised. 

The objective of this procedure is to help ensure that changes are properly reviewed and that hazards introduced by the implementation of the change are identified and controlled before the change is implemented. The management of change procedures should be used as the gatekeeper of the PSM program to ensure that as changes are made, the PSM program is modified as needed. 

 

At Kraft Heinz, all MOCs for ammonia refrigeration systems require review by operators and engineers (or a technical manager) and require management authorization prior to implementation. 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain Kraft Heinzs management of change procedures are contained in Element 10, Management of Change. 

 

Element 11 -Incident Investigation 

The purpose of investigating serious incidents and nearmiss

es is to understand what happened (or could have happened) and then to prevent any recurrence of similar incidents, thereby improving the safety of the process. 

A formal incident investigation must be performed any time there is an incident which resulted in, or which could reasonably have resulted in (nearmiss), a catastrophic release of ammonia. For the purpose of this guideline, a catastrophic release is defined as a major uncontrolled emission, fire, or explosion involving ammonia that presents serious danger to employees, the employees of contractors working onsite, or to offsite neighbors. 

The Kraft Heinz approach goes beyond the minimum requirements (because small occurrences can lead to larger ones), and Kraft Heinz wants to learn/improve from our experiences. The Kraft Heinz procedures include: 

 

Performing an immediate investigation when a small non-hazardous nuisance odor is reported, to determine the source of the odor. This type of investigation requires documentation of the reason for the odor and actions taken to correct the source of the odor. All affected and involved people, including the person who originally reported the odor and their manager, is required to sign off on a formal Nuisance Odor Report once the situation has been corrected. This document is required to be shared with the overall plant population. 

Incidents involving a release or catastrophic event, or incidents which could have potentially resulted in a release or catastrophic event beyond a nuisance odor will require the implementation of a formal Incident Investigation with a team of knowledgeable personnel. The incident will be fully investigated to learn the Root Cause(s) of the incident, and actions taken to prevent its recurrence. 

Lessons learned from incident investigations will be shared with all plant personnel and shared for the benefit of other Kraft Heinz facilities. 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain Kraft Heinzs incident invest

igation procedures are contained in Element 11, Incident Investigation. 

 

Element 12 -Emergency Planning and Response 

Written emergency response plans are required for all ammonia refrigeration facilities.  Facilities must designate at least one plant contact to interface with emergency responders. 

The emergency planning and response guidelines contain the emergency action plan requirements and the essential steps necessary to initiate, conduct, and terminate an emergency response action. 

 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain the Kraft Heinz emergency response plans are contained in Element 12, Emergency Planning and Response. These procedures must be consistent with other Emergency Guidelines for a specific facility. 

 

 

Element 13- Compliance Audits 

Kraft Heinz will perform an audit of its process safety management program at least once every thirty-six months (for regulatory compliance), and more frequently as warranted. Selfauditing is a cost effective, instructive, and positive approach to improving the safety of a process provided that the auditors are impartial to the process and management actively pursues implementation of audit recommendations. It is also a process that ensures continuous improvement is being made in safely operating and managing the Ammonia refrigeration systems at Kraft Heinz facilities. 

 

The steps involved in conducting a compliance audit are: 

Define the Audit Requirements 

Prepare for the Audit 

Conduct the Audit 

Report on the Audit Findings 

FollowUp on the Audit Findings 

 

Specific procedures that are followed to develop and maintain the Kraft Heinz compliance audit program are contained in Element 13, Compliance Audits. 

 

Element 14 - Trade Secrets 

Subject to the rules in the HazCom Standard, employees and their representatives shall have access to trade secret information in PHAs, and other documents required by the PSM Standard. The employer may, however, require employe

es to execute confidentiality agreements providing that trade secrets will not be disclosed. 

Kraft Heinz trade secrets policy is defined in Element 14, Trade Secrets. 

 

PSM Standard Maintenance 

The Ammonia Refrigeration Management System (ARMS) Process Safety Management (PSM) program is an evergreen system. As described above, the program has 14 PSM Elements, where each element contains various information in the form of either electronic and/or paper (hard copy) files/documents. The information in the PSM program must be kept current and accurate to comply with OSHA regulations. 

 

Facility Manager Responsibilities 

Facility management, specifically the Facility Manager, is responsible for the safety of the employees, contractors, and the surrounding population. Implementation of the PSM Standard is designed to reduce the risk to employees, contractors, and the surrounding population. To ensure proper implementation of the PSM Standard, the Facility Management will assign a PSM Coordinator and back-up PSM Coordinator from within the facility. 

 

PSM Coordinator Responsibilities 

It is the responsibility of the PSM Coordinator to ensure the PSM program is fully implemented and kept current. The PSM Coordinator will steward the implementation of the 14 PSM Elements and report deficiencies to Facility Management and appropriate corporate personnel. 

 

Typical tasks the PSM Coordinator will perform include: 

 

Schedule and coordinate Process Hazard Analysis. 

Facilitate annual certification of the Operating Procedures. 

Ensure training records are maintained for affected employees. 

Ensure annual review of ammonia refrigeration contractor qualifications (training and safety records). 

Ensure pre-startup safety reviews are completed, documented, and filed. 

Ensure ammonia refrigeration maintenance tests and inspections are performed to standard and documented properly. 

Facilitate the management of change process and ensure all documentation and t

raining is complete prior to implementation of the change. 

Coordinate PSM incident investigations and ensure recommendations are implemented in a timely manner. 

Coordinate PSM compliance audits and ensure recommendations are implemented in a timely manner. 

Kraft Heinz Corporate Responsibilities 

Kraft Heinz Corporate will support the PSM Coordinator and the Facility Management as needed to implement the PSM Standard. To ensure the PSM Standard if fully implemented, Kraft Heinz Corporate will help plan the PSM compliance audits and track progress on recommendations as needed. Kraft Heinz Corporate will also promote the implementation of best practices to ensure PSM Coordinators have the necessary knowledge, skills, and tools.
